title: Principles of Microeconomics
text:
Preface
Welcome to Principles of Microeconomics: An Institutional and Social Science Perspective.
This textbook offers an analytical, empirical approach to microeconomic decision-making, price theory, market structures, and policy evaluation. It is structured around the analytical depth of Eric Chiang (Microeconomics: Principles for a Changing World, 5th ed.) and UC Berkeley Econ 1.
Use the left sidebar navigation to explore individual chapters or press s to initiate full-text keyword searches across the entire volume.

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
text:
1.1 What Is Economics? Scarcity, Choice, and Method
Economics is the social science that studies how individuals, institutions, and societies allocate scarce resources among competing ends to satisfy unlimited human wants.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
text:
1.1.1 Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics

Microeconomics: Examines decision-making by individual units—such as households, workers, firms, and individual product and factor markets. It investigates how relative price signals coordinate supply and demand in specific sectors (e.g., electric vehicles or pharmaceutical labor).
Macroeconomics: Examines aggregate performance, focusing on national output (GDP), price instability (inflation), systemic labor underutilization (unemployment), and long-run secular growth.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
section: 1.2 Economic Modeling and the Ceteris Paribus Assumption
text:
1.2 Economic Modeling and the Ceteris Paribus Assumption
To analyze human behavior, economists formulate economic models—stylized, simplified representations of real-world phenomena that isolate cause-and-effect relationships by stripping away confounding variables.
\[\begin{equation}
Ceteris Paribus \equiv "All other things held constant"
\end{equation}\]
Economic models rely on assumptions (such as rational self-interest and net benefit optimization) not because humans are purely calculating machines, but because these abstractions yield predictable baseline tendencies across large populations.






TipReal-World Application: California Gasoline Taxes



When modeling the effect of an increase in the California gasoline excise tax on consumer fuel purchases, economists hold public transit availability, regional household income, and crude oil spot prices constant (ceteris paribus). In reality, transit routes and crude prices fluctuate simultaneously. Isolating the tax impact first establishes the clean directional policy response before introducing multi-variable empirical complexities.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
text:
1.3 Positive vs. Normative Economic Analysis
Clear economic discourse separates factual mechanics from ethical prescriptions:

Positive Economics: Descriptive statements regarding how the economy actually operates. Positive claims are empirical assertions that can be tested, confirmed, or refuted using observable data (e.g., “Increasing the statutory minimum wage to $20 per hour will reduce teenage employment by 2.4%”).
Normative Economics: Prescriptive statements regarding how the economy ought to be structured, incorporating ethical values and political priorities (e.g., “The government ought to increase the statutory minimum wage to $20 because every working individual deserves a living wage”).
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
section: 1.4 Critical Thinking Pitfalls in Economic Reasoning
text:
1.4 Critical Thinking Pitfalls in Economic Reasoning
When evaluating economic arguments, analysts must guard against three pervasive analytical traps:

Confusing Correlation with Causation: Presuming that because variables \(A\) and \(B\) move together, \(A\) causes \(B\) (e.g., ice cream sales and drownings both spike in July due to summer temperatures, not mutual causation).
The Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc Fallacy: Concluding that because event \(Y\) occurred sequentially after \(X\), \(X\) must have caused \(Y\).
The Fallacy of Composition: Mistakenly presuming that what is true for an individual component is automatically true for the aggregate whole.

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
section: 1.6 Core Principle 2 — Marginal Analysis and Rational Decision-Making
text:
1.6 Core Principle 2 — Marginal Analysis and Rational Decision-Making
Decisions are evaluated at the margin by weighing incremental benefits against incremental costs:

Marginal Benefit (MB): The additional satisfaction or revenue generated by consuming or producing one extra unit.
Marginal Cost (MC): The additional opportunity cost incurred by producing or consuming one extra unit.

Net Benefit Maximization Rule: Expand if \(MB > MC\); Halt where \(MB = MC\).






TipReal-World Example: Airline Seat Pricing



A commercial airliner with 180 seats has a total operating flight cost of $18,000 (average cost = $100 per seat). Ten minutes before departure, an unreserved seat remains empty, and a standby passenger offers $60. A manager fixated on average cost would reject the offer because $60 < $100. A rational marginal manager accepts the $60, recognizing that the marginal cost of carrying one extra passenger (a small snack and minor incremental jet fuel) is roughly $10. Because $MB ($60) > MC (\(10)\), selling the seat increases operating profits by $50.



[Graphical Model: Marginal Benefit intersects Marginal Cost at equilibrium \((Q^*, P^*)\)]
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
section: 1.5 Core Principle 3 — Response to Incentives and the Peltzman Effect
text:
1.5 Core Principle 3 — Response to Incentives and the Peltzman Effect
Agents adjust behavior when relative prices change. Mandating vehicular safety equipment in 1968 reduced the perceived risk of reckless driving, causing drivers to speed and brake later, increasing pedestrian collisions.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
section: 1.8 Core Principle 4 — Markets, Efficiency, and the Invisible Hand
text:
1.8 Core Principle 4 — Markets, Efficiency, and the Invisible Hand
As Adam Smith observed in The Wealth of Nations (1776), decentralized price signals guide self-interested agents toward productive and allocative efficiency:

Allocative Efficiency: Resources are distributed to produce the specific bundle of goods and services most highly valued by society (\(MB = MC\)).
Productive Efficiency: Goods are produced at the lowest possible per-unit cost using the most effective combinations of factor inputs.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
section: 1.9 Core Principle 5 — Market Failures and the Economic Role of Government
text:
1.9 Core Principle 5 — Market Failures and the Economic Role of Government
When decentralized private transactions fail to allocate resources efficiently, a market failure occurs, establishing an economic rationale for public intervention:

Externalities: Unpriced costs or benefits imposed on third parties (e.g., pollution or basic research).
Market Power: Firms restricting output to artificially inflate prices above marginal cost.
Public Goods: Non-excludable and non-rival goods subject to free-riding (e.g., national defense).
Efficiency vs. Equity Trade-off: Even perfectly efficient competitive markets can yield extreme inequality, requiring societies to balance allocative efficiency against distributive justice.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
text:
2.1.1 Core Assumptions of the PPF Framework

Resource Scarcity: Productive factors are strictly bounded during the period under examination.
Full and Efficient Employment: All factor inputs are actively engaged without operational waste or structural idling.
Fixed Technology: Engineering processes and organizational practices remain constant.
Two-Good Economy: Output is simplified to two alternative goods (or composite categories).
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.2 Opportunity Cost and the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost
text:
2.2 Opportunity Cost and the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost
Because resources are scarce, expanding the production of Good \(X\) requires diverting inputs away from Good \(Y\). The slope of the PPF measures the Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT): \[\begin{equation}
MRT = -\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X} = \left| \frac{dY}{dX} \right| = \frac{Quantity of Good  Y  Forgone}{Quantity of Good  X  Gained}
\end{equation}\]

2.2.1 Constant vs. Increasing Opportunity Cost

Constant Opportunity Cost (Linear PPF): Productive factors are perfectly interchangeable between both production processes. The slope remains constant along the frontier (\(MRT = k\)).
Increasing Opportunity Cost (Bowed-Out / Concave PPF): Productive resources are specialized. Shifting factors into Good \(X\) pulls inputs that are progressively less adapted to its production, causing opportunity costs to escalate.







TipEmpirical Case: Healthcare Facilities vs. Clean Energy Infrastructure



A regional economy allocates bonding capacity and engineering labor between Diagnostic Healthcare Facilities and Solar Energy Arrays. Initially, reallocating general electrical contractors efficiently constructs solar arrays. However, pushing exclusively toward solar requires reassigning specialized biomedical researchers and surgical nursing teams. Because these professionals possess a comparative disadvantage in manufacturing solar cells, the forgone healthcare services per megawatt rise exponentially, generating a bowed-out PPF.
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.3 Productive vs. Allocative Efficiency & Outward Shifts
text:
2.3 Productive vs. Allocative Efficiency & Outward Shifts

Productive Efficiency: Producing directly along the PPF curve at minimum opportunity cost.
Allocative Efficiency: The specific bundle on the PPF boundary where societal net marginal value is maximized (\(MB = MC\)).


2.3.1 Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Technological Shifts
General demographic growth or educational attainment expands the PPF symmetrically outward. In contrast, sector-specific innovation (e.g., robotic photolithography in semiconductor manufacturing) pivots the PPF outward along the affected axis while leaving the alternative intercept fixed.
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.4 Ricardian Comparative Advantage & Gains from Trade
text:
2.4 Ricardian Comparative Advantage & Gains from Trade
Opportunity cost determines comparative advantage. Voluntary exchange expands societal consumption possibilities beyond domestic production boundaries.






TipNumerical Case: Pacific Coast vs. Great Lakes Trade Matrix



Allocating a standardized 1,000-hour block of skilled labor yields the following outputs:

Pacific Coast: 100 Aircraft or 200 Turbines. \[Opportunity Cost of 1 Aircraft = 2.0 Turbines \quad (1 Turbine = 0.5 Aircraft)\]
Great Lakes: 40 Aircraft or 120 Turbines. \[Opportunity Cost of 1 Aircraft = 3.0 Turbines \quad (1 Turbine = 0.33 Aircraft)\]

Because \(2.0 < 3.0\), the Pacific Coast possesses a comparative advantage in Aircraft. Because \(0.33 < 0.5\), the Great Lakes holds a comparative advantage in Turbines.
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.5 The Terms of Trade and the Consumption Possibility Frontier (CPF)
text:
2.5 The Terms of Trade and the Consumption Possibility Frontier (CPF)
Mutually advantageous trade requires that the terms of trade (TOT) settle strictly between both domestic opportunity costs: \[\begin{equation}
2.0 Turbines < 1 Aircraft < 3.0 Turbines
\end{equation}\]
At an agreed exchange rate of \(1 Aircraft = 2.5 Turbines\):

The Pacific Coast exports 1 Aircraft (costing 2.0 turbines domestically) and receives 2.5 turbines, capturing a gain of \(+0.5\) turbines per transaction.
The Great Lakes imports 1 Aircraft for 2.5 turbines (saving 0.5 turbines compared to domestic production).

Both economies rotate their Consumption Possibilities Frontier (CPF) strictly beyond their domestic production possibilities.
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare
section: 4.2 Deadweight Loss of Price Controls and Taxes
text:
4.2 Deadweight Loss of Price Controls and Taxes
An excise tax \(t\) creates a tax wedge \(P_b - P_s = t\). Deadweight loss (\(DWL\)) follows Harberger’s triangle: \[\begin{equation}
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times t \times (Q^* - Q_t)
\end{equation}\] The economic incidence ratio depends on relative elasticities: \(\frac{\Delta P_b}{\Delta P_s} = \frac{\varepsilon_s}{|\varepsilon_d|}\).
crumbs: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare

title: 5  Chapter 5: Elasticity: Responsiveness of Demand and Supply
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5: Elasticity: Responsiveness of Demand and Supply

title: 5  Chapter 5: Elasticity: Responsiveness of Demand and Supply
text:
5.2 The Total Revenue Test
Total Revenue \(TR = P \times Q\). Differentiating with respect to price yields: \[\begin{equation}
\frac{d(TR)}{dP} = Q(1 - |\varepsilon_d|)
\end{equation}\] When demand is inelastic (\(|\varepsilon_d| < 1\)), price increases raise total revenue.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5: Elasticity: Responsiveness of Demand and Supply

title: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves
text:
6.1 Production Functions and Diminishing Returns
Output \(Q = f(L, \bar{K})\). The Marginal Product of Labor is \(MP_L = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta L}\). By the Law of Diminishing Marginal Productivity, \(\frac{d(MP_L)}{dL} < 0\).
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves

title: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves
text:
6.2 Cost Function Duality
Total Cost \(TC = FC + VC(Q)\). Marginal Cost \(MC = \frac{d(TC)}{dQ} = \frac{w}{MP_L}\). Average Total Cost \(ATC = AFC + AVC\). \(MC\) intersects \(ATC\) and \(AVC\) at their minimum points: \[\begin{equation}
\frac{d(ATC)}{dQ} = \frac{MC - ATC}{Q} = 0 \implies MC = ATC
\end{equation}\]
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves

title: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
text:
7.1 Price-Taking Equilibrium
Competitive firms face a horizontal demand curve at market price \(P = MR = AR\). The profit-maximizing condition is \(P = MC(q^*)\).
crumbs: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium

title: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
text:
NoteShutdown and Exit Decision Rules




Short-Run Shutdown: Produce if \(P \ge \min AVC\); shut down if \(P < \min AVC\).
Long-Run Exit: Stay in industry if \(P \ge \min ATC\); exit if \(P < \min ATC\).
crumbs: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
text:
8.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
After this chapter, students should be able to model a single-price monopolist’s output and price, calculate economic profit and deadweight loss in a linear example, and explain how market power differs from the mere presence of one seller. These objectives support C2001-1, C2001-2, and C2001-3.
Key terms include monopoly, entry barrier, marginal revenue, market power, price discrimination, consumer surplus, and deadweight loss.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
text:
8.5 Price Discrimination
Price discrimination means charging different prices for the same or similar product when the difference is not explained by a difference in marginal cost. It requires some ability to set price, a way to sort or identify buyers, and limits on resale between buyer groups. Student discounts, time-based fares, and quantity discounts are familiar examples, although their economic and legal details differ.
Under first-degree discrimination, a seller charges each buyer close to that buyer’s willingness to pay. In the idealized model, output can expand toward the efficient quantity while the seller captures most consumer surplus. Under third-degree discrimination, the seller separates observable groups and sets different prices; the group with less elastic demand generally faces the higher markup, provided marginal costs are comparable. Price discrimination can expand access for some buyers, but it can also transfer surplus from consumers to the seller. Its welfare effect depends on output, costs, and who receives the service.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
text:
9.1 Monopolistic Competition and Excess Capacity
Firms sell differentiated products with free entry. In long-run equilibrium, demand is tangent to downward-sloping \(ATC\), resulting in excess capacity: \(Q_{\text{actual}} < Q_{\text{efficient scale}}\).
crumbs: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
text:
9.2 Oligopoly and Game Theoretic Equilibrium
In concentrated markets, strategic interdependence governs pricing. In a \(2 \times 2\) Prisoner’s Dilemma, dominant strategies lead to a non-cooperative Nash Equilibrium where both firms defect, earning lower profits than cartel collusion.
crumbs: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
Students should distinguish private from social costs and benefits, solve for a simple efficient quantity, and compare corrective policy tools. These objectives support C2001-1 and C2001-2. Key terms include externality, marginal private cost, marginal social cost, Pigouvian tax, public good, common resource, free rider, and Coase bargaining.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.2 Typology of Goods

Private Goods: Excludable and Rivalrous.
Public Goods: Non-excludable and Non-rivalrous (Free-rider problem; optimal provision \(\sum MB_i = MC\)).
Common Resources: Non-excludable and Rivalrous (Tragedy of the Commons).
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

11.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
Students should represent a budget constraint, identify an affordable choice, and explain how prices and income shape a consumer’s decision. These objectives support C2001-1 and C2001-3. Key terms include budget set, utility, indifference curve, marginal utility, marginal rate of substitution, substitution effect, and income effect.

title: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination
text:
12.1 Derived Labor Demand
A competitive firm hires labor where Marginal Revenue Product equals the market wage: \[\begin{equation}
MRP_L = MP_L \times P = W
\end{equation}\]
crumbs: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination

title: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination
text:
12.2 Monopsony in Labor Markets
A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve, meaning Marginal Factor Cost exceeds the wage (\(MFC_L > W\)). The firm hires where \(MRP_L = MFC_L\) and pays wage \(W_m < MRP_L\), creating deadweight loss. Imposing a binding minimum wage can raise both wages and employment in monopsonies.
crumbs: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
13.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
Students should distinguish hidden information before a transaction from hidden actions after it, calculate expected value and expected utility in a simple risk problem, and evaluate screening, signaling, and contract design. These objectives support C2001-1, C2001-2, and C2001-3. Key terms include asymmetric information, adverse selection, signaling, screening, moral hazard, risk aversion, expected utility, and risk premium.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
Adverse Selection (Pre-contractual): Unobserved characteristics drive high-quality products out of the market (Akerlof’s Lemons Model). Mitigated via screening and Spence signaling.
Moral Hazard (Post-contractual): Hidden actions occur when an insured party takes excessive risks. Mitigated via deductibles and co-payments.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
text:
14.1 Free Trade Welfare Mechanics
Domestic prices converge to World Price \(P_w\). If \(P_w < P_d\), the nation imports, expanding consumer surplus by more than domestic producer surplus contracts.
crumbs: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
text:
14.2 Welfare Effects of Protectionism
A tariff \(t\) raises domestic price to \(P_w + t\):

Domestic consumer surplus falls by area \(A + B + C + D\).
Domestic producer surplus rises by area \(A\).
Government tariff revenue equals area \(C = t \times Imports\).
Deadweight loss equals production distortion \(B\) plus consumption distortion \(D\): \(DWL = B + D\).
crumbs: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism

title: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
text:
7.2 Shutdown and Exit Rules

Short-Run Shutdown: Produce if \(P \ge \min AVC\); halt if \(P < \min AVC\).
Long-Run Exit: Remain in market if \(P \ge \min ATC\); exit if \(P < \min ATC\).

In long-run equilibrium, free entry and exit enforce zero economic profit: \(P = MR = MC = \min ATC\).
crumbs: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text:
The Substitution Effect: As the price of a good rises, it becomes relatively more expensive compared to alternative goods, incentivizing consumers to substitute toward cheaper alternatives.
The Income Effect: A price increase erodes the consumer’s real purchasing power, constraining the total quantity of goods they can afford to purchase.


3.1.1 Direct vs. Inverse Demand
In empirical economics, demand is specified directly as quantity as a function of price: \[\begin{equation}
Q_d = a - bP \quad (a > 0, b > 0)
\end{equation}\] Because economists traditionally graph price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis (following Alfred Marshall), we invert the equation to obtain the Inverse Demand Function: \[\begin{equation}
P = \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}Q_d
\end{equation}\] Here, \(\frac{a}{b}\) represents the choke price—the price at which quantity demanded drops to exactly zero.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.2 Shifts in Demand vs. Movements Along the Demand Curve
text:
3.2 Shifts in Demand vs. Movements Along the Demand Curve






NoteCrucial Distinction: Demand vs. Quantity Demanded




Movement Along the Curve (Change in Quantity Demanded): Caused strictly by a change in the good’s own price.
Shift of the Entire Curve (Change in Demand): Caused by changes in non-price determinants, altering quantity demanded at every price level.




3.2.1 Non-Price Determinants of Demand

Consumer Income: For a normal good, demand shifts rightward as income expands (\(\varepsilon_I > 0\)). For an inferior good (such as instant ramen or intercity bus transit), demand shifts leftward as income rises (\(\varepsilon_I < 0\)).
Prices of Related Goods:
Substitutes: An increase in the price of Good \(Y\) shifts demand for Good \(X\) to the right (\(\varepsilon_{xy} > 0\)).
Complements: An increase in the price of Good \(Y\) shifts demand for Good \(X\) to the left (\(\varepsilon_{xy} < 0\)).
Tastes and Preferences: Exogenous shifts in consumer culture, health studies, or advertising.
Buyer Expectations: Anticipated future price increases prompt consumers to accelerate current purchases, shifting current demand rightward.
Market Demographics: An expansion in the population of potential buyers shifts market demand outward.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.3 The Nature of Supply and Marginal Opportunity Costs
text:
3.3 The Nature of Supply and Marginal Opportunity Costs
The Law of Supply establishes a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, ceteris paribus: \[\begin{equation}
P \uparrow \implies Q_s \uparrow, \qquad P \downarrow \implies Q_s \downarrow
\end{equation}\] Supply slopes upward because production is governed by the Law of Diminishing Marginal Productivity. As firms hire variable factor inputs into fixed plant capacity, the marginal product of labor declines, forcing marginal production costs (\(MC\)) to escalate. To cover higher incremental costs, firms require higher market prices.

3.3.1 Linear Supply Formulations
\[\begin{equation}
Q_s = c + dP \iff P = -\frac{c}{d} + \frac{1}{d}Q_s \quad (d > 0)
\end{equation}\]


3.3.2 Non-Price Determinants of Supply
Supply shifts when underlying production parameters change:

Input Prices: Wage increases, raw material inflation, or soaring energy costs increase marginal cost, shifting supply leftward.
Technological Progress: Cost-reducing manufacturing breakthroughs allow firms to produce more output at each price level, shifting supply rightward.
Government Taxes and Subsidies: An excise tax increases per-unit production cost, shifting supply vertically upward by the tax amount \(t\).
Number of Active Producers: Industry entry expands market supply; business closures contract it.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text:
3.4 Market Equilibrium and Price Discovery
A competitive market attains equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: \[\begin{equation}
Q_d(P^*) = Q_s(P^*) = Q^*
\end{equation}\]






TipStep-by-Step Algebraic Equilibrium Solution



Consider a regional agricultural market for specialty roasted coffee beans: \[Q_d = 500 - 15P, \qquad Q_s = -100 + 15P\] 1. Equate \(Q_d\) and \(Q_s\): \[500 - 15P = -100 + 15P \implies 30P = 600 \implies P^* = $20\] 2. Substitute $P^* = \(20\) into either direct schedule: \[Q^* = 500 - 15(20) = 500 - 300 = 200 \text{ bags}\] 3. Verify at disequilibrium prices:

If $P = \(25\) (Price too high): \(Q_d = 125\), \(Q_s = 275 \implies \text{Surplus} = +150\). Unsold inventory forces price downward.
If $P = \(15\) (Price too low): \(Q_d = 275\), \(Q_s = 125 \implies \text{Shortage} = -150\). Eager buyers bid price upward.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.5 Simultaneous Dual Shocks and the Indeterminacy Matrix
text:
3.5 Simultaneous Dual Shocks and the Indeterminacy Matrix
When demand and supply shift concurrently, exactly one equilibrium variable (\(P^*\) or \(Q^*\)) changes unambiguously, while the other is indeterminate without knowing the exact relative magnitudes of the shifts.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare
text:
4.2 Deadweight Loss of Taxation
An excise tax \(t\) creates a tax wedge \(P_b - P_s = t\). Deadweight loss follows Harberger’s formulation: \[\begin{equation}
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times t \times (Q^* - Q_t)
\end{equation}\] The relative tax incidence ratio depends on elasticities: \(\frac{\Delta P_b}{\Delta P_s} = \frac{\varepsilon_s}{|\varepsilon_d|}\).

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
text:
1.4 Core Principle 2 — Marginal Decision-Making
Rational agents optimize at the margin by weighing incremental benefits against incremental costs: \[\begin{equation}
\text{Optimization Rule: Expand if } MB > MC; \quad \text{Halt where } MB = MC
\end{equation}\]






TipReal-World Application: Airline Seat Pricing



A commercial aircraft has an average operating cost of $100 per seat. An unsold seat ten minutes before departure costs only $10 in marginal jet fuel and refreshments. Selling it to a standby passenger for $60 increases operating profit by $50 because \(MB\text{ ($60)} > MC\text{ ($10)}\).
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
text:
2.2 Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost
Concave curvature reflects imperfect factor adaptability. As resources shift toward one sector, inputs progressively less suited to that industry must be utilized, driving opportunity costs upward.
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves
text:
6.2 Cost Duality and Minimum Crossings
Total Cost \(TC = FC + VC(Q)\). Marginal Cost is inversely linked to productivity: \(MC = \frac{w}{MP_L}\). Average Total Cost \(ATC = AFC + AVC\). \(MC\) intersects \(ATC\) and \(AVC\) at their minimum points: \[\begin{equation}
\frac{d(ATC)}{dQ} = \frac{MC - ATC}{Q} = 0 \implies MC = ATC
\end{equation}\]
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
text:
9.2 Oligopoly Game Theory
Firms exhibit strategic interdependence. In a \(2 \times 2\) Prisoner’s Dilemma, dominant strategies lead to a non-cooperative Nash equilibrium where both firms discount, undercutting cartel profit.
crumbs: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory

title: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination
text:
12.2 Monopsony Power
A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply, so Marginal Factor Cost exceeds wage (\(MFC_L > W\)). Firms hire where \(MRP_L = MFC_L\) and pay \(W < MRP_L\). Binding minimum wages can raise both wage and employment under monopsony.
crumbs: 12  Chapter 12: Factor Markets, Labor Demand, and Wage Determination

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
text:
14.2 Tariffs and Quotas
A tariff \(t\) raises domestic price to \(P_w + t\). Consumer surplus falls by area \(A + B + C + D\), producer surplus expands by \(A\), and government tariff revenue equals \(C = t \times \text{Imports}\). Total societal deadweight loss equals \(DWL = B + D\).
crumbs: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
section: 8.2 A Scanner, a Local Market, and the Cost of Entry
text:
8.2 A Scanner, a Local Market, and the Cost of Entry
Consider a hospital deciding whether to operate an advanced diagnostic scanner. The equipment has a large fixed cost: it must be purchased, staffed, maintained, and kept available even when no patient is being scanned. Once installed, the marginal cost of one additional scan may be much smaller than the average cost at low volume. A nearby clinic considering entry must also recruit technicians, obtain regulatory approvals, and attract enough patients to cover its fixed costs.
This example helps distinguish scale economies from monopoly power. A scanner can lower average cost as its fixed cost is spread over more scans, but that fact alone does not establish that the hospital is a monopolist. We must define the relevant service and geographic market, identify reasonable substitutes, and examine whether entry is feasible. A patient may travel to another hospital, use a different diagnostic test, or defer a scan; each possibility changes the competitive constraint.






TipIllustrative Hospital Scanner Calculation



Suppose annualized fixed cost is $900,000 and the marginal cost of each scan is $100. At 3,000 scans per year, average total cost is $900{,}000/3{,}000 + 100 = \(400\) per scan. At 9,000 scans, it is $900{,}000/9{,}000 + 100 = \(200\). These values are illustrative, not hospital data. Higher volume lowers average cost over this range, but it does not by itself prove that the hospital can profitably raise price above the level constrained by alternatives.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
section: 8.3 The Demand Curve, Marginal Revenue, and the Graph
text:
8.3 The Demand Curve, Marginal Revenue, and the Graph
A competitive firm can sell another unit at the going market price without changing the price received on earlier units. A single-price monopolist cannot: to sell an additional unit, it generally must lower the price, and that lower price applies to all units sold. Therefore its marginal revenue lies below its demand curve.
In the standard graph, put quantity on the horizontal axis and price or cost per unit on the vertical axis. Draw a downward-sloping demand curve \(D\) and a marginal-revenue curve \(MR\) below it. Draw marginal cost \(MC\) rising or horizontal. The monopolist chooses the quantity at the intersection of \(MR\) and \(MC\), then moves vertically to the demand curve to find the price consumers will pay. Do not read the monopoly price from the \(MR=MC\) intersection: that intersection determines quantity, not price.
The competitive benchmark is the quantity where willingness to pay on demand equals marginal cost. With downward-sloping demand and the same marginal cost, the monopoly quantity is lower and its price is higher than that benchmark. The missing mutually beneficial trades between the two quantities are the source of deadweight loss.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
section: 8.4 A Linear Model: From Story to Equation
text:
8.4 A Linear Model: From Story to Equation
Let inverse demand be \(P(Q)=100-2Q\) and constant marginal cost be \(MC=20\), with no fixed cost in this numerical exercise. Total revenue is \(TR(Q)=P(Q)Q=100Q-2Q^2\). Differentiating gives \(MR(Q)=100-4Q\). The firm’s profit-maximizing condition is \(MR=MC\): \[\begin{equation}
100-4Q_M=20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_M=20, \qquad P_M=100-2(20)=60.
\end{equation}\] At this outcome, profit is \((P_M-MC)Q_M=(60-20)20=800\). The competitive quantity in this simplified model solves \(P=MC\), so \(100-2Q_C=20\), or \(Q_C=40\). Deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and marginal cost over the units from 20 to 40: \[\begin{equation}
DWL=\tfrac{1}{2}(Q_C-Q_M)(P_M-MC)=\tfrac{1}{2}(20)(40)=400.
\end{equation}\] The triangle formula assumes the linear curves used here. If curves are nonlinear, deadweight loss is the area between marginal social benefit and marginal cost over the underproduced units.
The Lerner index relates a firm’s price-cost margin to the absolute value of demand elasticity at the optimum, under the assumptions of a single-price profit-maximizing firm with an interior solution: \[\begin{equation}
L=\frac{P-MC}{P}=\frac{1}{|\varepsilon_d|}.
\end{equation}\] In the example, \(L=(60-20)/60=2/3\). A larger index signals a larger price-cost margin relative to price; it is not, by itself, a complete measure of consumer harm or a legal finding of anticompetitive conduct.






NoteClear It Up: One Seller Does Not Automatically Mean Monopoly Power



The number of firms in a narrow category is not enough to establish market power. The relevant market includes products and locations that buyers see as substitutes, and potential entry can constrain an incumbent even before a new firm opens. Conversely, several firms may still have substantial market power if they face weak competition.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
section: 8.6 A FRED Price Index Is Not a Monopoly Test
text:
8.6 A FRED Price Index Is Not a Monopoly Test
FRED series CPIMEDSL is the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: Medical Care in U.S. City Average. It is a monthly, seasonally adjusted index with base period 1982-1984=100. The September 2026 observation is 593.666. The index tracks the average price movement of a defined basket; it is not a price for a particular hospital scanner, a hospital’s marginal cost, or a measure of concentration. A rising index alone therefore cannot show that monopoly power caused medical-care inflation. To test that claim, researchers would also need evidence about product markets, entry, costs, quality, and substitutes.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
text:
8.7 Check Your Understanding

In the linear example, what price corresponds to the quantity where \(MR=MC\)? Why is the intersection itself not the monopoly price?
If the demand curve becomes more elastic at the optimum while marginal cost is unchanged, what does the Lerner relation predict about the percentage markup?
A hospital is the only provider of one scanner type in a town. Name two additional facts needed before concluding that it has market power in the relevant market.

Answers: (1) \(P=60\), read from demand at \(Q=20\); the \(MR=MC\) intersection identifies quantity. (2) The markup share \(L\) falls. (3) Examples include travel distance to substitutes, alternative diagnostic procedures, and the likelihood of entry.
crumbs: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
section: 10.2 A Neighborhood, a Plant, and Unpriced Costs
text:
10.2 A Neighborhood, a Plant, and Unpriced Costs
Imagine a production facility that releases pollution affecting nearby residents. The firm pays for labor, energy, and materials, but without a fee or regulation it may not pay for all health and environmental damage imposed on others. The firm’s private production decision can therefore differ from the decision that maximizes total surplus. The same logic applies to traffic congestion: one driver’s trip adds delay to other road users, a cost the driver may not fully consider.
An externality is a cost or benefit from an action that affects a third party outside the transaction. A negative externality creates a wedge between private and social cost; a positive externality creates a wedge between private and social benefit. Not every spillover is a market failure of equal size: measurement, the number of affected parties, property rights, and transaction costs matter.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.3 Negative Production Externalities: The Graph
For a negative production externality, place quantity on the horizontal axis and dollars per unit on the vertical axis. Draw marginal private cost (\(MPC\)) below marginal social cost (\(MSC\)), because \(MSC\) includes the damage borne by third parties. Draw marginal benefit (\(MB\)), assumed here to equal marginal private benefit. The unregulated market produces where \(MB=MPC\). The efficient quantity is where \(MB=MSC\); it is lower in this example. The vertical distance between \(MSC\) and \(MPC\) is marginal external cost (\(MEC\)). The overproduced units create deadweight loss between the benefit and social-cost curves.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.4 A Corrective-Tax Calculation
Suppose inverse marginal benefit is \(MB=100-Q\), marginal private cost is \(MPC=20+Q\), and marginal external cost is a constant 10 dollars per unit. Then \(MSC=MPC+MEC=30+Q\). The unregulated outcome satisfies \(100-Q=20+Q\), giving \(Q_M=40\). The efficient outcome satisfies \(100-Q=30+Q\), giving \(Q^*=35\). A per-unit tax equal to \(MEC(Q^*)=10\) makes the private decision face the social marginal cost at the efficient quantity: \[\begin{equation}
MB(Q^*)=MSC(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*)+t^*, \qquad t^*=MEC(Q^*)=10.
\end{equation}\] In this linear example, the deadweight loss from the five excess units is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(40-35)(10)=25\) dollars per period. The triangle formula depends on the linear, constant-damage assumptions; with changing damage, use the area between \(MB\) and \(MSC\).






TipFRED Data: Emissions Are Not a Damage Estimate



FRED series EMISSCO2TOTVTTTOUSA reports U.S. total carbon dioxide emissions from all sectors and fuels, in million metric tons, annually and not seasonally adjusted. It records 4,594.7 million metric tons in 2020 and 4,911.2 in 2021. These totals describe emissions, not the marginal health or climate damage from one additional unit, and the year-to-year rebound does not identify a single cause. Students should separate measured quantities from an external-cost estimate.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.5 Positive Externalities and Corrective Subsidies
Vaccination can reduce a recipient’s risk and lower transmission risk for others. If decision-makers consider only private benefit, participation may be below the socially efficient level. In a graph, marginal social benefit (\(MSB\)) lies above marginal private benefit (\(MPB\)). The market chooses where \(MPB=MC\); the efficient quantity satisfies \(MSB=MC\). A subsidy can encourage participation, but its design should account for fiscal cost, targeting, and the size of the spillover rather than assuming every private benefit deserves public payment.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.6 Public Goods and Common Resources
Goods can be classified by whether people can be excluded and whether one person’s use reduces another’s use. Private goods are excludable and rival; public goods are difficult to exclude people from and are non-rival over the relevant range. A lighthouse signal is a classic stylized example. Common resources are difficult to exclude users from but rival, such as a congested fishery. Club goods are excludable and largely non-rival until congestion, such as a subscription service.
The free-rider problem occurs when people can benefit without paying, making voluntary private provision difficult. For a pure public good, efficiency requires the sum of individuals’ marginal willingness to pay to equal marginal cost: \[\begin{equation}
\sum_i MB_i(Q^*)=MC(Q^*).
\end{equation}\] For a common resource, each user may ignore the congestion or depletion imposed on others. Property rights, access rules, tradable permits, or community management can help, but monitoring and enforcement have costs.






NoteClear It Up: A Tax Does Not Erase the Externality



A corrective tax changes private incentives; it does not make the physical damage disappear. The efficient tax is tied to marginal external damage at the efficient quantity under the model’s assumptions. Distribution, measurement error, and administrative costs still matter.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
10.7 Check Your Understanding

In the numerical example, why is the market quantity larger than the efficient quantity?
If marginal external damage rises with output, should the efficient tax necessarily equal the damage at the unregulated market quantity?
Give one example of a common resource and explain which of the two defining properties it has.

Answers: (1) Producers face \(MPC\) rather than the higher \(MSC\). (2) No; the Pigouvian tax is the marginal damage at the efficient quantity in the standard model. (3) A fishery is rival and difficult to exclude users from without enforceable access rules.
crumbs: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
section: 11.2 A Monthly Budget and Two Goods
text:
11.2 A Monthly Budget and Two Goods
Suppose a student allocates a fixed monthly budget between meals (\(X\)) and transit trips (\(Y\)). The budget is limited, so buying more of one good means giving up some of the other. The consumer’s choice depends on prices, income, and preferences; the model does not claim that every person calculates derivatives before buying lunch. It organizes the trade-offs implied by those constraints.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
text:
11.3 The Budget Line: Geometric Description
Place meals \(X\) on the horizontal axis and transit trips \(Y\) on the vertical axis. The budget line slopes downward. Its horizontal intercept is the number of meals affordable if all income is spent on meals; its vertical intercept is the number of transit trips affordable if all income is spent on transit. A rise in income shifts the budget line outward in parallel when prices are fixed. A change in one price pivots the line around the intercept for the other good.
The budget constraint is \[\begin{equation}
P_xX+P_yY=I, \qquad Y=\frac{I}{P_y}-\frac{P_x}{P_y}X.
\end{equation}\] The slope is \(-P_x/P_y\): it is the number of transit trips that must be forgone to purchase one more meal while staying on the same budget line.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
text:
11.4 Preferences, Utility, and Indifference Curves
An indifference curve collects bundles that provide the same ordinal utility. A higher curve represents a preferred bundle when preferences are monotonic. With well-behaved preferences, indifference curves slope downward and are convex to the origin: as a person has more of \(X\) relative to \(Y\), they are generally willing to give up fewer units of \(Y\) for another unit of \(X\).
Marginal utility (\(MU_x\)) is the change in utility from a small increase in \(X\), holding \(Y\) fixed. The marginal rate of substitution is the absolute slope of an indifference curve: \[\begin{equation}
MRS_{XY}=\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}.
\end{equation}\] Utility numbers are a representation for ranking choices, not a literal measurement of happiness that can be compared across people.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
section: 11.5 Choice at a Tangency: Worked Example
text:
11.5 Choice at a Tangency: Worked Example
Let income be \(I=60\), with \(P_x=4\) and \(P_y=3\). The consumer has Cobb-Douglas utility \(U(X,Y)=XY\). Since \(MU_x=Y\) and \(MU_y=X\), the tangency condition \(MRS=P_x/P_y\) implies \(Y/X=4/3\). Combining this with the budget constraint gives \(X^*=7.5\) meals and \(Y^*=10\) transit trips. The bundle exhausts the budget: \(4(7.5)+3(10)=60\).
For an interior optimum with smooth, convex preferences: \[\begin{equation}
\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=\frac{P_x}{P_y} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{MU_x}{P_x}=\frac{MU_y}{P_y}.
\end{equation}\] At a corner solution, the consumer chooses only one good; the tangency equality need not hold. Perfect substitutes, perfect complements, and nonstandard preferences can also change the shape of the solution.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
section: 11.6 Price Changes: Substitution and Income Effects
text:
11.6 Price Changes: Substitution and Income Effects
If the price of \(X\) falls, the budget line pivots outward along the \(X\) axis. The total change in the chosen amount of \(X\) can be separated conceptually into a substitution effect and an income effect. The substitution effect reflects the change in relative prices while holding purchasing power conceptually constant; the income effect reflects the change in real purchasing power. For a normal good, both effects of a price decrease usually raise quantity demanded. For an inferior good, the income effect works in the opposite direction and may partly offset the substitution effect. A parallel budget shift is caused by a change in income at fixed prices; it is not the price-change income effect itself.






NoteClear It Up: The Price Change Pivots the Budget Line



A change in \(P_x\) changes the budget line’s slope and rotates it around the \(Y\) intercept. A change in income shifts the entire budget line in parallel when both prices remain fixed. Keep these two geometric changes distinct.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
section: 11.7 FRED Data and Real Purchasing Power
text:
11.7 FRED Data and Real Purchasing Power
FRED series CPIAUCSL is the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average. It is monthly, seasonally adjusted, and indexed to 1982-1984=100; its September 2026 observation is 336.298. The CPI is a broad price index, not the exact cost of every household’s basket. It can help convert a nominal dollar amount to a broad real-dollar comparison, but it does not identify an individual’s preferences or their personal inflation rate.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves
text:
11.8 Check Your Understanding

With \(I=60\), \(P_x=4\), and \(P_y=3\), what are the two intercepts of the budget line?
Why does the budget line pivot rather than shift in parallel when only \(P_x\) changes?
Is utility measured in directly comparable units across people? Explain.

Answers: (1) \(X=15\) and \(Y=20\). (2) The \(X\) intercept changes while the \(Y\) intercept remains \(I/P_y\). (3) No; ordinal utility represents an individual’s ranking of bundles.
crumbs: 11  Chapter 11: Consumer Choice Theory: Utility and Indifference Curves

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
section: 13.2 A Used-Car Market with Hidden Quality
text:
13.2 A Used-Car Market with Hidden Quality
Imagine a market in which sellers know whether a used car is reliable, but buyers cannot observe its condition before purchase. Buyers offer a price based on expected quality across cars offered for sale. Owners of especially reliable cars may reject that pooled price and keep their vehicles. The remaining pool has lower average quality, so buyers reduce their offers again. This feedback can shrink the market or drive high-quality products out of it.
This is adverse selection: private information about a characteristic that exists before a contract affects who chooses to participate. It is not the same as a seller’s deliberate fraud; the problem can arise even when everyone behaves legally and rationally.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
section: 13.3 A Graph of Pooling and Market Unraveling
text:
13.3 A Graph of Pooling and Market Unraveling
In a price-quality diagram, put product quality on the horizontal axis and buyers’ willingness to pay on the vertical axis. If quality is hidden, buyers initially offer a pooled price reflecting expected quality. Sellers whose cars are worth more than that price to them exit first. The average quality of cars still offered falls, shifting buyers’ expected willingness to pay downward. A credible warranty, inspection, or reputation can make quality more observable and interrupt this unraveling process.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
13.4 Screening and Signaling
Screening is an action by the less-informed party to learn about hidden types. An insurer may ask risk-relevant questions or offer a menu of plans with different premiums and deductibles. Signaling is an action by the informed party intended to credibly reveal type. A warranty may signal seller confidence if it is more costly for a seller of an unreliable product to honor.
For a signal to separate types, it must be credible: the cost of sending it should differ across types. A signal everyone can imitate at negligible cost conveys little information. Screening and signaling can improve matching, but they can also exclude people, expose private information, or create administrative costs.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
13.5 Moral Hazard after a Contract
Moral hazard is a change in behavior after a contract when one party’s action is not fully observable or contractible. Insurance can reduce the cost of a loss to the insured person, which may change prevention effort or use of covered services. The effect is not necessarily fraud: it is a predictable response to changed incentives. Deductibles and co-payments can preserve some incentives to economize, but they also expose risk-averse households to more financial risk and may discourage valuable care.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
section: 13.6 Risk, Expected Value, and Expected Utility
text:
13.6 Risk, Expected Value, and Expected Utility
Suppose a household faces a 10 percent chance of a $1,000 loss and a 90 percent chance of no loss. The expected loss is $100. A risk-neutral person compares premiums with expected monetary loss. A risk-averse person has a concave utility function and may be willing to pay more than the expected loss for insurance, up to the risk premium, because a certain outcome can provide greater utility than a risky outcome with the same expected wealth.
For outcomes \(x_i\) with probabilities \(p_i\), expected value and expected utility are: \[\begin{equation}
E[X]=\sum_i p_ix_i, \qquad EU=\sum_i p_i u(W+x_i).
\end{equation}\] The certainty equivalent (\(CE\)) is the certain change in wealth that gives the same utility as the risky prospect. For a gain-risk representation, the risk premium is \(RP=E[X]-CE\). The sign and interpretation depend on how gains and losses are represented; the central lesson is that expected dollars and expected utility are different criteria.






TipFRED Data: Delinquency Is an Outcome, Not a Diagnosis



FRED series DRALACBS is the Delinquency Rate on All Loans at All Commercial Banks. It is quarterly, seasonally adjusted, and measured in percent; the Q2 2026 observation is 1.42 percent. This aggregate rate can motivate questions about credit risk, but it cannot by itself identify adverse selection, moral hazard, underwriting changes, borrower composition, or macroeconomic shocks as the cause. Identifying those mechanisms requires more detailed evidence and a credible comparison.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
13.7 Contract Design and Trade-Offs
Markets use warranties, certification, deductibles, co-payments, collateral, audits, and reputation systems to mitigate information problems. Each tool trades off information or incentive benefits against cost, privacy, access, and fairness. A policy that reduces one information problem can create another: extensive screening may improve risk classification while making essential coverage unaffordable to some households.






NoteClear It Up: Adverse Selection and Moral Hazard Differ by Timing



Adverse selection concerns hidden characteristics that affect participation before a contract is signed. Moral hazard concerns hidden actions or effort after a contract changes incentives. The same market can experience both, but the diagnosis and remedy differ.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design

title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
text:
13.8 Check Your Understanding

A buyer cannot distinguish reliable from unreliable sellers before purchase. Which mechanism can cause high-quality sellers to leave the market?
An insured driver takes less care after coverage begins. Is this adverse selection or moral hazard, and why?
For the 10 percent, $1,000-loss example, calculate expected loss. Does that number determine the maximum premium every risk-averse household will pay?

Answers: (1) Adverse selection. (2) Moral hazard because the behavior changes after the contract. (3) Expected loss is $100; risk preferences and the risk premium determine willingness to pay beyond it.
crumbs: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
